content: Six years after receiving funding, the sources of research funds were not considered to pose a conflict of interest for the development of this guideline. However, one individual, due to her extensive publications on the topic and authorship of systematic reviews used as evidence, refrained from participating in discussions and decision-making regarding the SQ-LNS recommendation. No other members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) declared any conflicts of interest, nor were any independently identified. Similarly, no members of the external peer review group or the systematic review teams declared any conflicts of interest, nor were any independently identified. The WHO guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children aged 6–23 months includes a detailed categorization of core food groups and subgroups. These include vegetables (e.g., cucumbers, onions, corn, mushrooms, turnips, iceberg lettuce, and others), dairy products (e.g., milk, yogurt, including fermented dairy like kefir or buttermilk, and cheese), and protein foods (e.g., eggs, legumes/pulses and their flours, soy foods, peanuts/groundnuts, tree nuts, seeds, and their pastes). Additionally, it includes various meats (e.g., beef, lamb, mutton, goat, game meat, pork, poultry, wild birds, and liver), fish (small fish eaten with bones and larger fish not eaten with bones), and added fats and oils (e.g., solid fats, highly saturated oils, and most unhydrogenated vegetable oils). Regarding milk consumption for children fed milk other than breast milk, the guideline compares animal milk to milk formula for children aged 6–11 months and animal milk to follow-up formula for children aged 12–23 months. The benefits of animal milk consumption are uncertain, while the harms are uncertain to moderate, with low certainty of evidence. The balance of evidence slightly favors milk formula for younger children and is uncertain for older children. Resource implications suggest large savings with animal milk consumption, but cost-effectiveness and acceptability vary. For unhealthy foods and beverages, the guideline evaluates the consumption of foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats, as well as sugar-sweetened beverages, non-sugar-sweetened beverages, and 100% fruit juice. No benefits were identified for greater consumption of these items, while harms were uncertain to moderate. The evidence certainty was low, and the balance of evidence favors reduced consumption of these foods and beverages. Cost-effectiveness and equity considerations generally favor reduced consumption, though variability exists. The guideline also addresses responsive feeding interventions, which include elements of caregiver responsiveness compared to interventions without these elements. The benefits of responsive feeding are moderate, with trivial or uncertain harms and moderate certainty of evidence. The balance of evidence favors responsive feeding, with moderate costs and probable cost-effectiveness. Acceptability and feasibility vary but are generally favorable.
